attachments.origin_landmark: pyramidal eminence on the posterior wall of the tympanic cavity

actions: tilts the stapes, reducing the amplitude of ossicular vibration

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: The smallest skeletal muscle in the body. Because its nerve leaves the facial nerve inside the facial canal, a facial palsy proximal to that branch adds HYPERACUSIS to the weakness -- which is how the lesion is localised above or below the stapedial branch.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Not an ultrasound-guided technique. Two distinct percutaneous/transcanal approaches described: (1) an external, blind percutaneous approach near the stylomastoid foramen (used for hemifacial-spasm-associated tinnitus, on the rationale that abnormal facial-nerve impulses drive stapedius spasm): insertion point 1 cm above the lower edge of the mastoid process, at the midpoint of the line connecting the mastoid process and the mandibular ramus; the needle is directed against the anterior edge of the mastoid process, adjusting direction if bone is contacted, to a depth of about 2.5-3 cm so the tip lies near the stylomastoid foramen (the toxin diffuses roughly 2-3 cm to reach the intratympanic stapedius, since no needle actually enters the middle ear this way); (2) a trans-canal microscopic/endoscopic middle-ear exploration with direct injection into the visualized stapedius muscle/tendon, used for middle ear myoclonus.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: External stylomastoid-foramen route: needle traverses skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia, the posterior edge of sternocleidomastoid, splenius capitis, and the posterior belly of digastric before reaching the injection depth near the foramen (needle no longer than 3 cm recommended). Trans-canal route: direct visualization of the middle ear via a transcanal microscopic/endoscopic approach places the needle tip on the stapedius muscle itself.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: External route: syringe aspirated before injection, proceeding only if no blood is returned, given proximity to the jugular bulb and (at more distance) the carotid artery. Trans-canal route: direct visualization of the stapedius tendon/muscle in the posterior tympanic cavity confirms placement.
structures_at_risk: facial nerve trunk and stylomastoid artery, as the nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen right at the target zone of the external approach
jugular foramen contents (internal jugular vein, glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves), close to the stylomastoid foramen
internal carotid artery, more distant but still a theoretical risk of a misdirected needle
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Two niche indications, neither a mainstream BoNT target: (1) tinnitus synchronized with facial spasms in hemifacial spasm -- an additional 5 U injection near the stylomastoid foramen (targeting stapedius) on top of routine facial BoNT injections produced a significantly higher subjective tinnitus improvement (76.9%) than 2.5 U (46.3%), in a large single-center retrospective series, with no injection-site complications reported; (2) middle ear myoclonus/stapedial myoclonus causing objective tinnitus -- a single case report describes direct trans-canal injection of BoNT into stapedius (and tensor tympani) as a temporary, reversible diagnostic/therapeutic trial before definitive tendon-sectioning surgery.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Zhu L, Pan L, Zhang X, Pan Y, Jin L, Teng F, 'Botulinum Toxin Type A Injection Near the Stylomastoid Foramen: A Safe and Effective Therapeutic Modality for Tinnitus in Patients With Hemifacial Spasm', Otol Neurotol 46(7):855-861 (2025), doi:10.1097/MAO.0000000000004542 -- retrieved via PubMed; Hutz MJ, Aasen MH, Kircher M, 'A Novel Technique for the Diagnosis and Management of Middle Ear Myoclonus', Laryngoscope 131:E248-E249 (2021), doi:10.1002/lary.28579 -- retrieved via PubMed.
